 Print this Article 
 View Comments Army veteran Maureen Gilbert was wearing patriotic earrings as on Boylston Street during the parade. She is the Junior Vice Commander of American Legion Post 16 in Mattapan. John Tlumacki/Globe Staff Under a cover of mist, which at times became rain, they marched. In true military fashion, hundreds of veterans, service members, and supporters in Boston’s annual Veterans Day Parade were undeterred by a little inclement weather. 
 “We embrace the suck, no matter what,” Army veteran Michelle Wright said, repeating a military motto. The smile on her face as she marched alongside fellow members of the North Atlantic States Regional Council of Carpenters Saturday afternoon suggested it wasn’t a hard task, despite the steady drizzle. 
 Active-duty service members, veterans organizations, ROTC groups, and regional marching bands all participated in the procession, which began at Copley Square and ended at City Hall Plaza. 
 The federal holiday, which is on Wednesday, honors those who have served in the U.S. armed forces. 
 Military advocacy groups, such as the North Atlantic States Regional Council of Carpenters, or American Legion posts — many of whom participated in Saturday’s event — provide veterans a familiar structure and support system, Wright said. 
 “They continue feeling like they are part of something ... It’s another brotherhood, another sisterhood that can continue,” Wright said. 
 The parade is also meaningful as a public display of gratitude towards those who have served, said David Perry, 60, of Jamaica Plain, who served 12 years in the Air Force. 
 “It means a lot to me,” Perry said. “It’s a way of saying thank you ... honor[ing] our military service members, future and past.” 
 Members of the Ancient and Honorable Artillery Company marched in the parade from Copley Square to Boston City Hall Plaza. John Tlumacki/Globe Staff Crew members of the USS Constitution gathered before the start of the parade. John Tlumacki/Globe Staff Tammy Myers, 66, who also served in Air Force, wore a hoodie reading “Veteran” instead of a uniform and watched the parade from the sidelines. But she, too, was incredibly moved by the demonstration “that people care.” 
 “It’s overwhelming,” said Myers, who traveled to Boston from Maine to watch her nephew march with the Maine Maritime Academy. “Gives me goosebumps.” 
 She and her sister, amid a crowd of other rain jackets and umbrellas, cheered as the young midshipmen filed down the street. The parade stretched up Boylston Street and curled left at Tremont before arriving at City Hall Plaza, where Mayor Michelle Wu and other city officials greeted the service members. 
 Commissioner Robert Santiago of the city’s Veterans Services department led the flag-raising ceremony. He and City Councilor Ed Flynn, both Navy veterans, invited veterans in the crowd to join them in hoisting the flag into the misty sky. 
 “To see so many people come out, regardless of the weather ... it means everything. It means the world,” Santiago said after the ceremony. “It doesn’t rain on the Veterans Parade!” 
 Santiago said he felt “honored” to serve Boston’s veterans — “to ensure that my fellow veterans are taken care of.” 
 But it was also moving to “see this outpouring of support ... as a veteran myself,” he continued. 
 “It just shows us that [Boston] is the premier city, as far as I’m concerned, that takes care of the veterans.” 
 Flags were thrown in the air by the Danvers High School marching band as the parade started in Copley Square. John Tlumacki/Globe Staff Members of the English High School Junior ROTC program were ready for the start of the parade. John Tlumacki/Globe Staff Spectators lined Boylston Street in Copley Square for the parade. John Tlumacki/Globe Staff
